content:
A reply to Dmitry Non's post “Common Lisp is a Dumpster”

This post was originally just going to be an email but got out of hand in scope so I published it here lol. I'd recommend reading Dmitry's post, there's good points and some interesting obscure stuff mentioned in there.

Intro and Outro

I think that it’s too old and got a lot of baggage that’s not of any use to someone like me. It feels like the authors just glued together a bunch of different programming languages together and made it a lisp.… but to me it feels wrong to go out of your way in order to keep backward compatibility with a bunch of old software. Not to mention, I’m sure they still had to do a bunch of work in order to migrate from previous implementations to Common Lisp.

Talking about it they still had to do a bunch of work in order to migrate from previous implementations to Common Lisp. One of the main drivers behind Common Lisp was to allow you to take code you wrote on your PC or VAX and run it on a Lisp Machine without needing to rewrite or modify it and vice-versa, which was actually realized because Symbolics added a Common Lisp wrapper; and you could get Common Lisp implementations, or Lisp implementations with a Common Lisp compatibility layer, for any platform academics would've been using at the time. So write once, run anywhere, a decade before Java! So they were very successful, it was so successful in fact that all the Lisp dialects that Common Lisp was compatible with died out, and now no one understands how valuable the compatibility was for CL's adoption.

Continuing that though and about it being too old, one thing I love about CL is that I can take pretty complex code I wrote for a modern implementation without compatibility in mind, and have run it literally unmodified on an implementation from 1992.1 And that implementation (Macintosh Common Lisp) was actually written before ANSI Common Lisp was even standardized, so it was based on Common Lisp the Language 2 (1990).

Finally, I'd say the language never officially changing or being updated has created a very high-quality developer culture. For instance, Common Lisp typically uses Quicklisp for dependency management, which autodownloads dependencies like NPM/Cargo and also absolutely sucks ass on an actually unprecedented level (you can't even specify a dependency version, it's always just the latest version).

And yet, despite not even being able to pin library versions, everything still works fine with even fewer issues than with NPM or Cargo, because the community actively avoids breaking changes and minimizes dependencies. Like, I can't recall encountering a CL program or library that doesn't build and run, even ones that haven't been updated since 2007, even if they use dependencies that still get regularly updated. (And modern programs can depend on those unmaintained libraries just fine as well). Excellent forward and backward compatibility, although unfortunately with newer waves of developers this seems to be changing and libraries aren't as trustworthy to stay stable and working long-term anymore.

Okay, moving on to infodumping about most of the specific points.

PROG and Friends

Nowadays PROG (more TAGBODY & BLOCK in particular) are useful for writing novel control flow macros, because just gotos lets you jump around however you want. For example, the popular ITERATE and FOR macros expand into a TAGBODY, rather than LOOP or DO or something like one may initially think. And even outside of macros, BLOCK is mildly useful to allow returns within an expression—although actually seeing BLOCK itself is rare because most standard control flow macros like DO & family already have implicit `(BLOCK NIL ,body) wrappers to allow using RETURN, and all named functions (i.e. defined in a DEFUN, FLET, or LABELS) already have `(BLOCK ,function-name ,body) wrappers to allow using RETURN-FROM.

However, prog1 and prog2 don’t seem to bring anything to the table. Their behaviour can be achieved with a simple let.

PROG1 is actually fairly useful because it lets you skip having to name a binding and then remember to add its symbol at the end to return it, if all you need is to do something like create an object, then do some auxiliary side-effect stuff. I use it off and on, useful for macros to save you from having to create yet another gensym, and in situations where UNWIND-PROTECT doesn't make sense. At the very least, it saves you from the LET indenting the body of the variable declaration further to the right, and avoids making the most important subexpression in a form be in the declaration area, a mild source of annoyance for me.

PROG2 is very rare but I know I've used it some time before… I think it was when GUI programming, to do some setup that must be done first in the first expression, create a window or rendering context or whatever in the second, then memoize some stuff in global variables, then return the rendering context? But nothing that you couldn't just do with a (PROGN ,setup (PROG1 ,create-thing ,other-work)), and that form would allow you to have more than one expression in the setup code too.

Assignment

SET is very important for some fancy functions, because otherwise you'd be forced to make them macros (with a loss of clarity of what the underlying function is actually doing) to allow expanding a variable to the quoted form required for SETQ or SETF. Some things would just be impossible without SET, once you start getting into complex dynamic stuff (ab)using facilities like symbols and packages for your own uses.

But yeah, I just use SETF for everything and do agree that most others are redundant. Although I like the things that wrap SETF such as INCF, since they follow SETF semantics (supporting custom setf expanders and such) while making common tasks easier. I have my own!

T and NIL

As for T and NIL… Well, T is confusing because it's one symbol/name that refers to multiple distinct things; and NIL is confusing because it's one object that acts as multiple distinct things.

Glossing over all the stuff already mentioned in Dmitry's post:

  • T is a constant value in the language that represents true. The T value, along with the NIL value, are the only two BOOLEAN types. Most conditional forms take a generalized boolean that means any non-NIL value is true, while the BOOLEAN type only allows the values T and NIL.
  • T is also symbol that evaluates to the constant value T, represented by the symbol T by the printer and reader, so functionally equivalent to the constant value T for everyone but someone hacking on the internals of an implementation. It is also just used as an arbitrary placeholder/catch-all where it doesn't matter what the symbol actually expands to, such as in (FORMAT T ...) or as the fallback clause in CASE & family. Note that since T is true, then it being the last value in COND isn't a special case, since any other truthy constant value would work; but it is a special value for CASE.
  • The type T is unrelated (just uses the same symbol to name it), and it is the root type that all other types and classes are derived from. Sorta like Java's Object type, except most Common Lisp types aren't classes (despite having standardized class-like inheritance) since CLOS was bolted on later. Having T in a type declaration is using the T symbol above to refer to the T type, without actually expanding to the value T; in the same way that the type named by the symbol NULL is distinct from the function bound to NULL. Note that like with COND, T being the fallback case for TYPECASE also isn't a special hardcoded case, since everything in the language is a subtype of T.
  • The class T is unrelated to the type T, and it is the root of all CLOS classes only. This means that deriving a class from T will skip things like the MOP STANDARD-CLASS that is the default class to inherit from, but isn't breaking out of the CLOS class hierarchy entirely like if you could derive from the ultimate root type T, since that's not a class. Unless you're digging into the deep internal workings of the Meta-Object Protocol, for all intents and purposes this is the same as the type T (and they likely are the same for implementations that have CLOS more tightly integrated into their internals).

NIL is actually both the empty list and the only falsy generalized boolean, but performs both of those functions using the same singular constant. Although note that NIL isn't specifically a BOOLEAN type, NIL is actually specified as the subtype of all other types, which just happens to include the BOOLEAN type. I suppose this is done just to allow storing NIL in any place (variable) even if you've declared the type of it and forgot to write (OR type NULL)? Also, sorta like the symbol T, NIL is just a symbol—or a special case in the reader for the case of ()—that represents and evaluates to the underlying NIL constant.

Iteration

Not much to add about the higher-order mapping routines (functions that take another function, rather than being an iteration macro) except that MAP can actually act as a side-effect–only iterator like MAPC but generic over any SEQUENCE, by specifying the result type as NIL. I'd say they're all very useful since they don't end up having overlap in what you use them for in practice (other than (MAP NIL) and MAPC; and also LOOP as a whole).

I also of course have my own mapping function; a destructive, non-consing version of MAPCAR in the vein of NCONC and NREVERSE and other N-prefixed list functions. I like the destructive versions as a trivial way to satisfy my microoptimization urges without changing much either way2.

I’ve already mentioned the loop macro above. But I think it deserves a special place in my personal hell.… I’m not advocating for removal or anything. In fact, I think it’s a pretty good feature. But it’s overly complex and I prefer to keep things simple. I never use it in my own code unless I’m worried about performance.

I alternate between avoiding LOOP at all costs and using it for all iteration, although at this point I've settled on using it for any situation where the higher-order mapping functions or the non-clunky other macros like DOLIST aren't suitable. It does particularly shine for really complex iteration that isn't possible to simplify, that would just unavoidably turn into nested spaghetti in other languages.

Generally, I prefer using recursion and dolist.

Always very sad that Common Lisp doesn't have standardized tail-call optimization because it makes me avoid using recursion for stack safety and portability reasons, even though AFAIK literally every extant implementation supports tail-call optimization other than ABCL that runs on the JVM. I would still use other iteration strategies most of the time for the sake of clarity, but there are a lot of situations where the recursive implementation is more clear than an iterative implementation.

Printing

Most of the functions listed in Dmitry's post are lower-level routines that are indirectly called by FORMAT (searching for format probably would've been more fruitful than searching for print) or the printer or the pretty-printer. Just read the CLHS on the printer and reader.

Also PRINT-UNREADABLE-OBJECT isn't actually a printing routine on its own, it's a nice wrapper routine when writing a custom PRINT-OBJECT method. It's guaranteed to print a class object in a way that will never be accidentally read as gibberish by READ, while letting you print the contents to allow friendly reading. For example, Practical Common Lisp chapter 23 demonstrates the structure of most PRINT-OBJECT definitions:

(defmethod print-object ((object word-feature) stream)
  (print-unreadable-object (object stream :type t)
    (with-slots (word ham-count spam-count) object
      (format stream "~s :hams ~d :spams ~d" word ham-count spam-count))))

Property Lists

The property list of symbols are definitely very rarely used, as is the fact that symbols are just arbitrary interned strings rather than special names that are only useful when bound to a value. I personally love using symbols as interned strings for very string-heavy programs (for example) for the same efficiency reasons that Java and some other languages by default intern all strings automatically.

Using the property list is nice for attaching metadata to an arbitrary symbol, most often used by complex macros to help keep track of bookkeeping for names the user defines. I think Practical Common Lisp chapter 24 demonstrates a use of this.

Also, mostly unrelated, plugging a post I wrote on the history of alists and plists in Lisp:

Some Inconsequential Lisp History; or, the Story of Associative Lists

Multiple Return Values

I absolutely adore multiple return values for a number of reasons and use them often, although they're unfortunately very clunky to use without wrapper macros in every Lisp dialect I've used. I of course have my custom BIND macro that makes capturing multiple values just as convenient as capturing single values. Nicer than abusing a list as a tuple to return, and not like list destructuring with DESTRUCTURING-BIND is any less verbose or clunky than using MULTIPLE-VALUE-BIND.

My only complaint about using multiple values is that LOOP very frustratingly has no way to bind multiple values, despite having a facility for list destructuring. So you have to write routines to directly return lists or wrap calls in MULTIPLE-VALUE-LIST only to immediately re-destructure it.

Asterisked Bindings

The practical reasons for separate LET and LET* forms (and similarly DO and DO*) are weak, but I really like them just to communicate and enforce that these things aren't dependent on each other. In the same way declaring something as constant in other languages isn't required (although does allow for optimizations), but is very important to communicate that a value isn't changed. And I think having the more restrictive version by default is a good default, in the same way Rust makes variables constant by default which helps prevent accidental mutation.

I explicitly put in a decent amount of work on my previously linked binding macro to ensure there's a BIND that always binds fully in parallel, and a separate BIND* for binding in order.

Naming

I didn't mention it but I particularly agree with Dmitry's complaints on function naming. I don't mind reading or writing it in code, but I really mind that it makes discoverability of things you don't already know about very difficult. Many cases where I just write a bunch of trivial routines for a project, and then six months later I end up incidentally stumbling across routines doing exactly what I needed built into Common Lisp, but with nonsense names I never would've found on my own. Although that's also sorta the fault of there being no apropos facility to search the descriptions of everything in the Common Lisp HyperSpec, you can only really search by name or category. Even for things that don't have C-style names that are abbreviated beyond comprehensibility, Common Lisp was created so long ago (and derived from Lisps that are even older) that things just don't have the names a modern programmer is used to for things, particularly for functional programming related things.

Overall, I can understand all the places Dmitry comes from, but can also see how the Common Lisp designers finalized their choices and I think it's pretty reasonable. But I am also unusual, I highly value stability and portability in my programming languages and libraries, while other programmers seem to universally prefer continually updated and improved monocultural implementations (not that those are inherently bad, but it just makes maintaining things long-term frustrating for me). And unlike Scheme, the spec is rich enough to not need to pull in implementation extensions or tons of external libraries for most code, and minimizing dependencies is pretty important for easy maintainability too.

I think it helps that since Common Lisp exposes so much of the internals of things and that it's so stable, you can always just write your own macro/function set that just replaces all the stuff you don't like, or just some of it piecemeal. Don't like LOOP? Just use ITERATE or FOR that have different syntax while offering much of the same capability! Don't like whatever control flow macros or mapping functions there are? Just write your own! Want to just rename all the janky stuff or put them in a nice package hierarchy? You can just have packages that imports all of COMMON-LISP, and then re-exports a subset, possibly under different names. In Lisp you generally aren't stuck with whatever the language designers and implementers deigned to give you thirty-five years ago.

  1. just with a custom loader script since ASDF 3 (c. 2013) obviously isn't built-in, and is too tied to the internals of implementations to trivially port. ↩︎

  2. with a generational garbage collector, a little extra consing incurs almost literally zero overhead so avoiding creating a few dozen short-lived 128-bit cons cells doesn't change much. ↩︎
